implementation_notes: container/heap is a protocol, not a type: you implement heap.Interface (Len, Less, Swap, Push, Pop) on your own slice type, and container/heap supplies heap.Init (Floyd's build), heap.Push, heap.Pop, heap.Fix, and heap.Remove. That shape is Go's idiom - the standard library supplies the algorithm and the caller supplies the type - and it is why there is no ready-made priority queue in the core. heap.Fix(h, i) after mutating an element in place is the in-place update path, and it is cheaper than pop-then-push. Note that heap.Pop calls your Pop method, which must remove the last element of the slice, not the root: that is the standard's convention and getting it wrong produces a heap whose root is arbitrary.
idiom_name: container/heap implementing heap.Interface on your own slice type
pitfalls: heap.Pop calls your Pop method, which must remove and return the LAST slice element - the library has already moved the root there. Removing the root yourself produces a heap with an arbitrary root.
The heap is not concurrency-safe: wrap it with a mutex, and be aware that the lock is held for the whole operation.
For Less, note Go's comparison direction: Less(i, j) means 'i has higher priority', so returning priority > gives a min-heap.
heap.Remove and heap.Fix require the index field to be maintained in Swap; without it, removal is impossible.
